c.tagline: Gateway to the Amazon, where a jungle opera house meets the meeting of the waters.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are metered but agreeing an approximate fare beforehand is common, especially from the airport; ride apps (Uber, 99) are widely used and usually cheaper.

emergency.note: 190 reaches the Military Police, 192 the SAMU ambulance service, and 193 the fire department.

avoid.reason: Caution in the port/centre and peripheral neighborhoods at night

hood_desc: The historic heart on the Rio Negro waterfront, home to the pink Teatro Amazonas opera house, the Mercado Adolpho Lisboa market and the old port; best for first-timers who want the landmarks and belle-epoque grandeur within walking distance.

Manaus's riverside leisure district, with a lively beach boardwalk, an amphitheatre, hotels and a strip of bars and restaurants that fill up at sunset; suits travellers who want nightlife and river views.
An affluent, modern neighbourhood of shopping malls, upscale restaurants and cocktail bars just north of the centre; good for visitors who want comfortable dining and going out close to hand.
A leafy, well-to-do central district with hospitals, business hotels and quieter tree-lined streets; a calm, convenient base a short hop from both the centre and Adrianopolis.

A traditional, working-class neighbourhood next to the centre, known for its local markets, family-run eateries and everyday Manaus life; suits budget travellers wanting an authentic, less touristy feel.

water.note: Stick to bottled or filtered water.

transit.hours: City buses run roughly 5:00 AM to midnight; river boats and ferries keep their own schedules, with far more departures by day.
transit.note: Manaus has no metro or tram - the city relies on an integrated municipal bus network (SINETRAM), while boats and ferries on the Rio Negro and Amazon connect river communities and neighbouring towns.
transit.pay: City bus fares are paid in cash to the onboard conductor or with the rechargeable PassaFacil card; boat fares are paid at the dock.

landmarks: Teatro Amazonas
This opulent Belle Époque opera house, built at the height of the rubber boom deep in the Amazon jungle, is Manaus's most photographed and iconic symbol.
Meeting of Waters (Encontro das Águas)
The dramatic sight of the dark Rio Negro and sandy-colored Amazon River flowing side by side for kilometers without mixing is one of nature's most striking visual phenomena.
Ponte Rio Negro (Rio Negro Bridge)
This striking cable-stayed bridge spanning the Rio Negro offers a sweeping modern silhouette against the Amazon skyline, especially dramatic at sunset.
Mercado Municipal Adolpho Lisboa
This ornate iron-and-glass market building, inspired by Paris's Les Halles, is a colorful hub of Amazonian produce, fish, and crafts right on the riverfront.
Museu do Seringal Vila Paraíso
A restored rubber-baron estate reachable by boat, offering an evocative glimpse into the rubber-boom era architecture set against dense rainforest.
Palácio Rio Negro
A grand early-20th-century mansion built by a German rubber trader, now a cultural center showcasing Manaus's elegant boom-era architecture.
Igreja de São Sebastião
A striking neoclassical church on a picturesque praça paved with black-and-white stone patterns evoking ocean waves, a favorite historic photo spot.
Museu da Amazônia (MUSA)
A rainforest reserve with a soaring canopy observation tower offering panoramic views over the unbroken Amazon jungle canopy.
Amazonas Sambódromo (Sambadrome)
A striking modern arena hosting Manaus's vibrant Boi-Bumbá and carnival festivities, notable for its bold contemporary architecture.
Anavilhanas Archipelago
One of the world's largest freshwater archipelagos, a maze of forested islands on the Rio Negro accessible from Manaus, offering iconic aerial and boat views of the Amazon.

train.note: There is no railway anywhere in the Amazon basin around Manaus, and Brazil runs no intercity passenger trains. The city is not connected by paved road to the rest of the country either, so travel means the river or the air.

bus.note: No international coaches, and very few useful domestic ones - Manaus is effectively a road island. The BR-174 north to Boa Vista and on toward Venezuela is the one long-distance route, served by Eucatur from the Rodoviária; the road east to Belém does not exist. For almost every other destination you fly or take a boat.

ferry.note: The Amazon is the highway here. Slow double-decker riverboats leave from the Manaus Moderna and Roadway terminals near the centre; you sling a hammock on deck or pay more for a cabin, and journeys are measured in days. The upriver trip to Tabatinga is the practical overland route into Colombia and Peru at the three-way frontier, where you clear immigration on arrival. Tickets are bought at the port a day or two ahead, not online, and speedboats (lanchas) cover the shorter legs faster for more money.

half.name: Janauari Ecological Park
half.blurb: A floodplain reserve on the Rio Negro with a floating village, home to giant Victoria Amazonica water lilies and caimans.

full.name: Presidente Figueiredo
full.blurb: A rainforest town of waterfalls and caves about two and a half hours north, known locally as the land of waterfalls.

full.name: Novo Airão
full.blurb: A riverside town on the Rio Negro where visitors swim with wild pink river dolphins that gather near the docks.
